accuracy.evidence: Placement checked against NC Mathematics (2013) Y2 (solve problems with addition and subtraction; recall and use multiplication facts in contexts) and Y3 (solve problems, including missing number problems, using number facts) and the EEF (2021) metacognition guidance, recommendation 2 (teach pupils to plan, monitor and evaluate). Every sum in the lab and items was worked by hand: 9+4=13, 9−4=5 for both take-away asks, 3 cats × 4 legs = 12, 7p < 9p so not enough (2p short), 10p ≥ 8p and 7p; the shell asks in Change the ask give 13, 5, Tom and 'no, 2 more'. Parameterised answers n+k, n-k (n ≥ 10 > k ≤ 6, and n ≥ 9 > k ≤ 8), n*k and n-k+2 stay positive whole numbers at every range corner (the items gate checks them).

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the documented word-problem slips named in the adult text: adding every number in sight (predict 'Add 8 and 5', challenge tag 'add', FIT '13' and '16p' cards), reading 'more' as add when 'how many more' asks for a difference (SORT card refusal 'More does not always mean add', p1, m2), copying a fact as the answer (tapping 8 or 5 is refused as 'a fact you will use', FIT '3 cats', tag 'fact', m6), the wrong kind of answer (FIT '13' and '5' for who, tag 'type', p3) and answering a different question (tag 'other', 'how many flew away' challenge, m4).

lab_distinct.evidence: flagreadq is built on the question text itself: the child taps individual words of a word problem to mark the ask, sorts four asks that share the same 9 and 4 into a method, and matches answers to the kind of answer asked for. flagqw (158 Question words) sorts who/what/where question words for English sentences, flagexam (178) is GCSE command words and timing, and flagmeaning (220) is reading-for-sense; none uses fixed numbers with changing asks or word-level marking of a maths question.

lab_teaches.evidence: The routine is discovered by doing: tapping a number says it is a fact, not the ask, so the child looks for the asking words; dropping 'How many more shells' into Add is refused with 'more does not always mean add', so the child sees the same 9 and 4 needing different methods; picking 13 for 'Who read more?' is refused because who needs a name. Change the ask then lets the child see one story give 13, 5, Tom and 'no' as the ask changes. Done messages state the rule after each scene.

predictions.evidence: Three predictions each with a tempting wrong option the lab disproves: 'Add 8 and 5' (the first question asks how many more, a difference), 'Yes, 9 and 4 make 13' (two of the four asks give 5 and are refused in Add), and 'A number' for who read more (13 and 5 are refused; Ana is the answer).

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six rotating challenge questions; wrong options carry five tagged messages that each name the slip: add (adding every number is a guess, read the ask first), fact (that number is a fact from the story), type (who wants a name, not a number), check (compare the money with the price, then say yes or no) and other (that answers a different question). In-scene refusals also name the slip per card (e.g. '7 adds 4 and 3. Each cat has 4 legs, so count 4, 8, 12').

readability.evidence: Kid paragraphs are four short paragraphs of plain sentences (facts and an ask, read it two times, say it in your own words, check the answer fits) within the family kid limit checked by validate_lessons.py; canvas text is one-word chips, a one-line banner and short question cards that wrap to at most three lines at 360 px. Curriculum terms (total, difference, method, metacognition) stay in the adult text, which passes the adult limit.

no_filler.evidence: Each kid paragraph teaches one step of the routine (facts vs ask, mark the ask, own words and method, answer fits). Adult paragraphs give the NC and EEF placement with key words, the four-part routine, five named mistakes with a caution about rushing, and what each lab scene does. The content gate's filler-phrase and 12% duplicate checks pass.

mobile.evidence: Checked on 360 px screenshots in light and dark: word chips are at least 44 px tall and 40 px wide and wrap onto four centred rows, the four shell cards sit in a 2 × 2 grid above two 166 px Add and Take away boxes with the answer shown on its own line once placed, the three answer cards span the width at 57 px tall, and the four ask pads fit two columns; nothing is clipped. The iPhone 13 walkthrough completes every Show me.

accessibility.evidence: Every canvas action has a labelled button twin: one 'Mark the word …' button per word, Pick each question then Put it in Add or Take away, one button per answer card in the two pick scenes, and one 'Ask: …' button per question in Change the ask. The canvas aria-label speaks every question, refusal and success; axe WCAG 2.1 AA runs clean in light and dark themes on desktop and iPhone 13.

sources: DfE (2013) National Curriculum in England: Mathematics programmes of study, Year 2 and Year 3 addition, subtraction and multiplication problem solving
EEF (2021) Metacognition and Self-Regulated Learning: guidance report, recommendations 1 and 2 (plan, monitor, evaluate)
NCETM (2014) Mastery: bar models and word problems guidance on reading the structure of a problem before choosing an operation
Polya, G. (1945) How to Solve It: understand the problem (what is the unknown?) before devising a plan
